title: Iambic pentameter: the heartbeat of Shakespeare's lines
examples: Why did Shakespeare write in iambic pentameter?

explain.say: Put your hand on your chest. Feel your heart? da-DUM, da-DUM. Shakespeare built many of his lines on exactly that beat. Look at the wave on the board: each da-DUM is a soft beat, then a strong one.

draw.text: Iambic pentameter: the heartbeat of Shakespeare's lines

explain.say: One da-DUM pair is called an iamb. Say it: i-amb. Listen to this line: but SOFT, what LIGHT through YON-der WIN-dow BREAKS. Can you hear the strong beats? Soft, light, yon, win, breaks.

Now count them. Look at the board: pen, tam, e, ter. Penta means five, and metre means measure. So pentameter means five measures: five da-DUMs, ten syllables in a line. Can you count the syllables on your fingers?

draw.name: x-word
draw.note: penta means five, meter means measure

explain.say: Back to the wave. Shall I comPARE thee TO a SUMmer's DAY? Ten syllables, five strong beats. Iambic pentameter often sounds like natural speech with a gentle rhythm, which is why actors find it easy to say. Does it sound like talking to you?

Superb! Here is the clever part: Shakespeare sometimes breaks the beat on purpose, to show a character is upset or confused. Look at the wave again. Challenge: in To be or not to be, that is the question, count the syllables. You will find eleven!

faq.a: Iambic pentameter is a line of ten syllables made of five iambs, five pairs of a soft beat then a strong beat: da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM.
An iamb is a pair of syllables, soft then strong, like the word a-WAY or be-CAUSE.

faq.q: Why did Shakespeare write in iambic pentameter?
faq.a: It is close to the natural rhythm of English speech but gives lines a steady beat that helps actors remember them and makes speeches sound grand.
Blank verse is unrhymed iambic pentameter. Most of Shakespeare's plays are written in blank verse, with some prose and some rhyme.

faq.q: Why does Shakespeare break the rhythm?
faq.a: A change in the beat makes you notice a line. He often breaks it when a character is upset, or uses prose for comic or ordinary characters.

facts: Shall I compare thee to a summer's day? opens Shakespeare's Sonnet 18 and is a line of iambic pentameter.
To be or not to be, that is the question has eleven syllables, with an extra soft ending.
